title: She Always Thought She Was a Citizen. Now She Faces a Voting Charge
summary:
Marva Cook always believed she was an American citizen. Now, at 66, she has learned otherwise, and she has been charged with voting illegally.

Cook lives in Syracuse, New York, and was adopted as a toddler. She told Homeland Security investigators earlier this month that she had always assumed she was born in the United States. But while searching for her biological mother, she said, she discovered she had a German birth certificate.

Federal prosecutors say Cook has held a green card for several years. They say she still cast ballots in recent elections even though she was not a citizen. She faces a single federal charge of voting by a noncitizen, tied to her vote in the 2022 midterm elections. She turned herself in and appeared in court on Wednesday. She declined to discuss the case, but said the court appearance was difficult and thanked the community members who came to court with her.

The case is one of the latest arrests highlighted by the Trump administration as it searches for noncitizen voters ahead of the midterms. Its own investigations, though, have shown such cases are incredibly rare and have not changed election outcomes.

Cook's supporters describe her very differently. She starred on Syracuse University's women's basketball team decades ago, leading the team in scoring in 1979-80 with 15 points per game, and she holds the school record for steals in a single season. Today she works as the YMCA's community school program director, supporting low-income families and young people. Her pastor, Fred Daley, said she is an active church member who for years dressed up as the church's Easter Bunny, and a longtime parishioner called her a person of service.
why_it_matters: It shows why it matters to check important papers and rules carefully, even when you think you already know the answer.

background_read: In the United States, only citizens are allowed to vote in federal elections.
A green card lets a person live and work in the country, but it does not make that person a citizen.
A person's birth certificate and adoption papers can decide what citizenship they hold, and sometimes grown-ups only learn the answer much later in life.
